title: Listening with the words
hook: follow the Gurmukhi and its meaning as the hymn is sung

segments.voice: Yesterday, rahao, the pause line at a hymn's center. Your line was pause here.

A film in a language you don't speak, with subtitles. At first your eyes race along the bottom of the screen and miss the faces. Then something shifts: the actor's voice breaks just as the words go by, and the two lock together. Not reading, not listening, but both at once, and the scene hits twice as hard. Many gurdwaras today have something similar. On a screen near the front, as the hymn is sung, the Gurmukhi words appear line by line; under them, the sounds in English letters; under that, a translation.
screen: `SUBTITLES THAT CLICK.` → `THE VOICE AND THE WORDS LOCK.` → `THE SCREEN NEAR THE FRONT.`

segments.voice: For four days you've practiced listening: just listening, then the mood of the raag, the instruments, the rahao line. Today adds the words. As a shabad is sung, follow along: the Gurmukhi if you can read it, the sounds if you can't, and the meaning either way. Why bother? Because for Sikhs, the music is never just music. Guru Ram Das says in the Guru Granth Sahib, in paraphrase: the Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word, and within the Word is all the nectar. The raag carries the mood; the words carry the teaching. Hear both at once, and the hymn can reach all of you. Often, the first time, you lose your place. The singer repeats a line you weren't expecting, or jumps back to the rahao, and your eyes are three lines behind. That's normal; kirtan repeats on purpose. Let the rahao be your anchor: when you're lost, look for it, because the singers will come back to it. Some Sikhs who grew up outside Punjab say this is how they came to know the Granth. Not in a classroom, but on Sunday mornings, reading along with the screen, line by line, year after year, until one day a line in Gurmukhi meant something without the translation. And you don't need the gurdwara for this. Apps and websites show the Gurmukhi, the sounds and a translation together, and many recordings are easy to follow along with.
screen: `FOUR DAYS OF LISTENING, THEN WORDS.` · `THE WORD IS THE GURU.` · `LOST? FIND THE RAHAO.` · `LINE BY LINE, YEAR AFTER YEAR.` · then, large: `SOUND AND SENSE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: If you can, play one shabad with its words open beside it, in Gurmukhi, in English letters and in translation, and follow along once, letting your eyes move with the voice. When you lose your place, don't stop the music; wait for the rahao line to come back. If you can't play one right now, read a single line of a shabad aloud, slowly, then its meaning, then the line again.
Rahao, the line a shabad returns to again and again, the anchor to find your place when you get lost following along.
Your line: sound and sense together. The raag brings the mood; the words bring the teaching. That's day one hundred eight.

howItsDone: Many gurdwaras display the words of the shabad being sung on a screen, in Gurmukhi with transliteration and translation, and Sikhs at home often follow along using apps or printed gutkas.
